title: Air Alert hack — the phone apps that faked nuclear danger in Ukraine and Russia
hooks: A phone app warned Kyiv of nuclear radiation. None existed.
Two countries at war got fake nuclear alerts in one weekend.
Ukraine's air raid app was hacked. Then Russia's was too.
'Don't worry, the Oreshnik is coming,' said a hacked alert app.
The app people trust for real missiles started lying.

scenes.narration: [serious] A phone app warned Kyiv of nuclear radiation. None existed. It was Ukraine's official air raid app.
Late Sunday, November 1, phones lit up.
First, radiation. Then a chemical threat. Then street fighting. One even said, the Oreshnik is coming. A Russian missile.
The Air Force said: there is no radiation threat. The app was paused.
But here's the strange part. By Monday, Russia said its own emergency app was hacked too. Fake nuclear warheads, launched at every region.
Who did it? One post named Hitcore. Nothing is proven.
Two countries at war. Both scared by a phone app.

visuals.at: Both scared by a phone app

facts.claim: Ukraine's emergency alert app was targeted by a cyberattack late Sunday Nov 1, 2026; residents got messages of high nuclear radiation danger in Kyiv, a chemical threat and public disturbances; the app was temporarily suspended and restored overnight

The app is Air Alert, an officially supported app made with the Digital Transformation Ministry and Ajax Systems; warnings included nuclear, chemical and street fighting threats; the Air Force said 'There is no radiation threat!' and that the app was likely compromised by the enemy
One message (in Russian) read: 'There will be a nuclear alert across all of Ukraine right now! Don't worry, the Oreshnik is coming!'
Oreshnik is a Russian missile; Air Alert users got a fake alert about an alleged Oreshnik launch
Russian officials said on Monday Nov 2 hackers sent fake alerts via the Emergency Ministry's mobile app; the ministry did not name the attackers and said the wider public alert system worked normally
The Russian fake alerts claimed nuclear warheads had been launched toward all Russian regions; MChS app breached on the night of November 2
One false post mentioned the hacking group Hitcore; Russian Telegram channel Mash said Hitcore claimed responsibility; AP could not verify it
